subject: Copywriting
title: The Newsletter Renaissance
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Newsletter Renaissance.

hook.text: In 2020, Substack turned email newsletters into a $1 billion business.

buildup.text: Social media algorithms hide your content from followers. Email delivers directly. No algorithm, no middleman.

discovery.text: Morning Brew grew to 4 million subscribers and sold for $75 million. A daily email newsletter became a media empire.

twist.text: The newsletter boom made email cool again. The same channel everyone declared dead in 2015 became the hottest in 2021.

climax.text: Email newsletters prove one thing: owned audience beats rented audience.

punchline.text: Email was declared dead. Then newsletters made billions.

quiz.question: How much did Morning Brew sell for?

details.summary: Email newsletters experienced a dramatic revival in the 2020s as platforms like Substack, Beehiiv, and ConvertKit empowered individual writers to build media businesses. Newsletters became the new blogs — owned channels where creators could build direct relationships without algorithmic...
details.whyItMatters: The newsletter renaissance proved that email is not a dying channel but an evolving one. Understanding this shift helps writers and brands leverage newsletters as both content and revenue platforms.
takeaways: Platforms like Substack made newsletter publishing accessible to anyone
Top newsletter writers earn six and seven figures from subscriptions
Newsletters offer algorithmic independence that social platforms cannot

faq.question: Why did newsletters become popular again in the 2020s?
faq.answer: Social media algorithm changes made it harder to reach audiences organically. Writers and creators turned to email because it offers direct, unfiltered access to subscribers. Platforms like Substack simplified publishing and added paid subscription tools.

faq.question: Can a newsletter really become a full-time business?
faq.answer: Yes. Writers like Emily Atkin (Heated), Casey Newton (Platformer), and Heather Cox Richardson (Letters from an American) earn substantial incomes from paid subscribers. The model works when writers deliver consistent, valuable content to engaged niche audiences.
